IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01833

We are therefore not dealing with idle fancy or empty fantasies. His interpretation of verse 8:12—“When God said to the Angels: I shall be with you. Strengthen those who believe”—discovers in every detail of the verse an allusion to the wâqi’a taking place in “each mystery of the seven mysteries,” that is, in each subtle organ or latîfa. Spiritual realities and lived states undoubtedly take shape in images or in lights whose particular qualities vary from one mystic to another. This is because everyone has a spiritual countenance of his own, distinguishing him in the “world of mystery,” just as his individual face distinguishes him in the sensory world.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01834
Yet the essential visionary event is shared by all. Semnâni records both findings repeatedly in the scattered passages of his Spiritual Diary:
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01835

“Often, at the beginning of my spiritual life, I had this thought: perhaps what you behold during the wâqi’a belongs to you alone. How, then, can you claim that it has value for everyone? My shaykh directed me to the spiritual guidance of those traveling the mystical path (irshâd al-sâlikîn). He instructed me to keep them company in retreat and to interpret their visions.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01836

“I then learned that at every mystical station (maqâm) through which I myself had passed, they too had undergone encounters with the supersensible (wâqi’ât) and direct visions (moshâhadât) corresponding to mine exactly, as closely as the feathers of an arrow resemble one another. Through them I thus acquired complete certainty that this path (tarîqat) is true, and that whoever travels it arrives at what all the mystics have reached.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01837

Ideally, we would gather here every fragment of the Spiritual Diary scattered through Semnâni's works, including all the visions reported by spiritual seekers. The veils change in opacity and transparency as the colored lights appear: the “colors of the veils of the seven mysteries,” the seven subtle centers. Semnâni never ceases to attend to them, faithfully continuing the Central Asian Sufi tradition inherited from Najmoddîn Kobrâ.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01838

In the latîfa qâlabîya, the mystic sees a dark blackness—not an indistinguishable void, but “a light the color of black smoke.” Depending on whether the element of Earth, Water, or Air predominates within him, he sees mountain peaks either clouded or clear.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01839

In the latîfa nafsîya, the light is blue. As he progresses from the nafs ammâra, the state of the flesh-bound, commanding soul, toward the nafs motma’yanna, the soul at peace and purified, the clouds obstructing the sky break apart. He sees a star-filled heaven; the stars seem to descend toward him, acting upon him as they will, and temptations recede.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01840

In the latîfa qalbîya, the light is red. Seven phases correspond to the seven degrees of the heart, each with its own visionary encounters (wâqi’ât) and symbols. The bond with the flesh-bound soul is broken; the heart is free. The light of pre-eternal Eros now predominates within the mystic, at the very center where his “spiritual child,” his true Self, begins to form.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01841
In the latîfa sirrîya, the light is white. The realities of the “world of mystery” begin to appear, together with fragrances subtler than anything the senses can smell.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01842

In the latîfa rûhîya, the light is yellow. According to the mystic's capacity to receive them, Angels and the Spirits of prophets become manifest. When he is firmly established at this station (maqâm), his own Spirit, his own “Angel,” manifests itself to him (tajallî al-rûh). From this we must begin to sense what the latîfa jabra’îlîya might be: the “Gabriel of your being,” as he appears in the pure mirror of the latîfat al-anâ’îya, the subtle center of your true Self.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01843

Each of the five stations marked by these first five latîfas has its own paradise, with castles, houris, and angels. Entry into them depends on the efforts of the disciple (morîd) under the direction of his shaykh. But the disciple cannot rise beyond them without the aid of divine attraction.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01844

The latîfa khafîya is the place and organ of the theophanies—manifestations—of the divine Names and Attributes. They are already so numerous for each mystic that no one could count them. The lights of the preceding five centers may appear here with heightened intensity, but the light peculiar to the circle of this latîfa is luminous black (aswad nûrânî).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01845

Finally, the latîfa haqqîya, the “mystery of mysteries,” is the place and organ of the theophanies of the divine Essence. In its existence before this world, in the world of Spirits before descending into the world of bodies, the soul contemplated what it now contemplates at this mystical station. That is why the Sufis say that the color of this “station of mystery” is a brilliant green: visio smaragdina, the emerald vision. “From it we departed [in our pre-existence], and to it we finally return.” We should add that devotional acts, intuitive perceptions, and contemplative stations also each have their own color.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01846

The growth of the subtle body, announced by a supersensible perception of the aura or colored Light belonging to each latîfa, corresponds to a penetration into the depths of the seven hidden meanings of the Qur'an—a penetration Semnâni pursues in his Tafsîr. The celebrated saying (hadîth) of the Prophet speaks of seven esoteric depths, or even seventy, seventy thousand, and so on: amid these multiplications, the number seven retains its qualitative significance. This recalls another, equally famous saying attributed to the Prophet: “God has seventy thousand veils of light and darkness.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01847

Semnâni confirms that the saying refers to the veils encountered (wâqi’a) within the seven latîfas. Each has ten thousand veils of light. Beyond them is the supreme Veil, which is Light itself, as the Prophet indicates when he says: “His Veil is light,” or “His Veil is fire.” These successive veils are attributes of the soul, forms of its mode of being through which, from one latîfa to another, it perceives minerals, plants, animals, the celestial Spheres, houris, and Angels, until it reaches the Pen, the destination of its heavenly ascent, its mi’râj.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01848

The mystic's own effort can carry him no farther; what is needed now is the attractive force of theophanic ecstasy (jadhba tajallîya). Semnâni deliberately uses the word mi’râj, for the Prophet's ecstatic ascent is precisely the model for the mystic rising through the successive heavens of his own being. And this brings us again to the question of the relationship between the subtle center Semnâni calls the “angel Gabriel of your being” (latîfa jabra’îlîya) and the “Muhammad of your being.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01849

Is this Gabriel to the inward Muhammad what the angel Gabriel was to the historical Muhammad? Or what walâyat, spiritual guardianship or intimacy with God, was to the Prophet's prophetic charisma (nobowwat)? Can we hope to find among the scattered passages of Semnâni's Spiritual Diary some indication that would let us go beyond what we suggested earlier (§3): namely, that the “Gabriel of your being” might be identical with the personal, supersensible guide (ostâd-e ghaybî), the “witness in Heaven” described by Najm Kobrâ and his school? Although Semnâni holds back just when we hope for a decisive statement, we can glean a few clues by reading certain passages together.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01850

In one group, he asserts that he has seen his Rûh, his “Angel,” in language similar to Najm Kobrâ's account of seeing his shaykh al-ghayb, his unseen spiritual guide. These passages must then be read alongside those in which Semnâni interprets the Qur'anic surahs describing the Prophet's first visions of the angel Gabriel. We find that whenever Semnâni recounts his own vision in his Diarium, and acknowledges how deeply it disturbed him, he appeals to the Prophet's example, since the Prophet's vision of the Angel had caused the same disturbance.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01851

Semnâni's “inner prophetology” thus identifies the two experiences. This identification brings us into contact with the hidden meaning of the prophetic gift itself, for the “Muhammad of your being” is the inner reality of outward prophecy. To reach that hidden meaning would, by that very fact, mean reaching walâyat, the “Imam of your being.” Yet Semnâni's reserve allows us to do no more than ask these questions.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01852

First, there are the passages in which our shaykh's interpretation finds an inner meaning in the Qur'anic account of the Prophet's vision of Gabriel. Above all, these are his commentaries on surah 53, the Star, and surah 81, the Folding Up of the Sun. The Book “is nothing but a revelation given to him; the One mighty in power taught it to him” (53:4–5)—that is, the angel Gabriel, the trustworthy Angel who serves as the organ of Revelation (amîn al-wahy).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01853

Semnâni comments: “Your portion of this in the world of your soul, O traveler of the mystical path”—that is, your personal share in the Angel's revelation, the hidden meaning of that revelation for you—“is to understand that God has placed within you the divine subtle organ, the ‘Muhammad of your being,’ and that this latîfa is the prophet within you who summons to God all the other subtle organs of your being: those at the level of the body, the vital soul, the heart, the innermost heart, the spirit, and the hidden mystery, together with all their faculties.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01854

The following verses of the surah, by indicating the height of the horizon where the Angel stands, allow the inward interpretation to take a decisive step forward: within you there is a latîfa higher than the “Muhammad of your being.” “The Angel stood at the highest horizon” (53:7), when he paused, upright and still. For each latîfa, Semnâni explains, has two horizons: one facing what is above it and the other facing what is below it. This corresponds exactly to the teaching of Shiite theosophy concerning the Haqîqat mohammadîya, the Muhammadan Reality, with its two “dimensions”: the one turned toward created beings is nobowwat, prophecy; the one turned toward God is walâyat.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01855

Thus each “prophet of your being” has a double horizon: below him, toward the prophet he succeeds; above him, toward the prophet who succeeds him. In the same way, minerals open onto the horizon of plants, plants onto that of animals, and animals onto that of human beings. The “Muhammad of your being” is therefore the supreme height of the horizon for the six preceding latîfas: their highest horizon.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01856

But his own highest horizon lies above him. It is the horizon at which the Angel is seen, a vision evoked first in surah 53 and then in surah 81: “The Qur'an is the word of the noble Messenger, obeyed and trustworthy. No, your companion is not mad. He saw him at the clear, translucent horizon (al-ofq al-mobîn)” (81:19–23). The “Muhammad of your being” beholds the Angel appearing at the “translucent horizon”—a horizon higher than himself, although he is the highest horizon of the six other latîfas.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01857

Unfortunately, on at least three occasions, we find Semnâni observing ketmân, the discipline of concealing a secret, at precisely this decisive point. In his commentary on surah 81, he writes: “Within the inner reality (haqîqat) of the horizon is a secret suspended at the boundary (hadd) of the Qur'an, something it is not permitted to disclose.” Earlier, commenting on surah 53:7, he had written: “Examine the two horizons. Strive to receive directly from the divine Being at the translucent horizon, without an intermediary. Do not be content with leftovers. Do not seek nourishment beneath your own level.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01858

“Yet no one can be nourished from his own self (min dhâti-hi) until he has reached the Self of the primordial Unity of unities (al-dhât al-wâhida, the Intelligence) and plunged into it. To understand this secret, one would have to knock at a door I have been ordered to keep closed. So pass on, and meditate.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01859

A third passage speaks more plainly of the latîfa jabra’îlîya, only to refuse just as firmly to say more. Verse 53:8 declares: “Then he drew near and remained suspended. He was at the distance of two bows.” For Semnâni, we should emphasize, the subject of the sentence is not the Angel, as almost all commentators suppose, but the Prophet—and thereby the “Muhammad of your being.” He accordingly writes:
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01860

“Understand, O mystic, that the divine subtle organ within you, your latîfa haqqîya, draws near to the divine Being. It remains suspended, stretching from the horizon of pre-eternity to that of eternity-to-come, until the latter meets the former. I mean that the expression ‘at the distance of two bows’ alludes to the two notches of the bow meeting when the archer draws it to its utmost tension. The words, and what they hint at, refer here to the latîfa haqqîya reaching the divine Being, at a boundary no one may cross. Everything the mofassirûn, the commentators, explain about the Prophet seeing Gabriel, the Angel's form covering the whole horizon, is entirely correct and true.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01861

“But then we must understand properly what the latîfa jabra’îlîya, the angel Gabriel of your being, is; what the horizon is; how the Angel's form covered the horizon; and what ‘covering the horizon’ means. The inner realities (haqâ’iq) of all this are suspended at the boundary (haqq) of the Qur'an. This is something that may not be explained explicitly in a commentary.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01862
“To understand what the latîfa jabra’îlîya is”: that is indeed the question on which the meaning and substance of this mystical experience depend.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01863

But since Semnâni refuses to answer it directly, we can only try to glimpse his secret in other remarks. They suggest how a vision in which the divine becomes manifest must, as such, be an angelophany: an appearance of the Angel, when what had previously disclosed itself to the mystic only invisibly takes on the reality of a visible face. And they suggest how the appearance of the Angel compels an inward interpretation through ta’wîl to posit a subtle center higher than the other seven latîfas. “The heart cannot deny what it saw” (53:11), and the Angel of Revelation had already been seen by Muhammad “another time, at the Lotus of the Utmost Boundary, where the Garden of Abiding is” (53:13–15). Our shaykh comments:
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01864

“Here again, everything the exoteric interpreters (ahl al-zâhir) say about the Lotus of the Utmost Boundary is true. Every mystic, in the course of his mi’râj, therefore contemplates something resembling what they describe.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01865

“Yet you must understand this: the Garden of Abiding certainly exists already, today, but it is with you. If you cultivate it and sow the seeds of paradise there, it will become your supreme Refuge. Hell exists, too, but it is with you; if you cultivate it and sow hell's seeds there, it will become your Gehenna.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01866

“Paradise and hell are at the Lotus of the Utmost Boundary. Every human being has a Lotus of the Utmost Boundary, because it is the outermost limit of the heart's secret (sirr), and he cannot go beyond it. Those seized by ecstasy, however, are drawn beyond the Lotus by the magnetic force of grace. For it is impossible for a human being to pass beyond the Lotus by his own action: every action is conditioned by the one who performs it.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01867
“Thus no one reaches God by his works, but only through divine assistance, and by being carried away through that assistance.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01868

“Every human being has a Lotus of the Utmost Boundary.” Perhaps that is the best and most discreet answer to the question, “What is the latîfa jabra’îlîya?” For every human being there is an Angel appearing at that Lotus, appearing to the “Muhammad of his being,” just as the Angel appeared to the Prophet. To pass beyond this Lotus, this boundary, is therefore to pass beyond the Angel of the theophany “who covers the whole horizon.” It is to pass beyond one's own paradise, to go beyond oneself.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01869

No human being can accomplish that by his own power. The Angel standing at the Lotus of the Utmost Boundary announces, by his very presence, something about which the mystic must remain silent. That is why the first vision, or the first few visions, of the Angel may so profoundly shake the visionary that he believes himself to have gone mad. We find an admission of this kind in Semnâni's Diarium. By identifying his own vision of “his Angel” with the Prophet's vision, he helps us sense more clearly what the latîfa jabra’îlîya is.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01870

Here we meet once more concepts and mystical images that have appeared throughout this book. For the gnostics, ubique et semper—everywhere and always—have sought and experienced one and the same reality: the transcendent archetypal Image, the heavenly Self, the divine alter ego, the companion who has existed since before time, and so on. All these themes are brought together and recalled in Semnâni's pages on the Rûh, the Spirit, and on the visionary experience of his own Rûh, his “Angel.” The Rûh, he explains, is a “subtle luminous substance” (jawhar nûrânî latîf) shaped in human form (mosawwar bi-sûrat âdamîya).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01871

Each person's Rûh is shaped like that person's body—or rather, to put it more precisely, the reverse is true: the Spirit is the archetype in whose image the body is formed. Semnâni understands the famous saying “God created Adam in His image” (’alâ sûrati-hi, “according to his form”) to mean that God created Adam's material body in the image, or according to the form, of Adam's Rûh. We might say that the Rûh, the personal spirit or angel, corresponds here to the Mazdean idea of the fravarti (forûhar). The Rûh, however, belongs to the “world of the immediate divine Command” (’âlam al-Amr), not to the world of mediated creation (’âlam al-khalq).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01872

Its first manifestation (tajallî) blossoms at the level of the subtle organ bearing its very name: the latîfa rûhîya, the “David of your being.” But there is more. The Rûh reveals itself differently at each of the higher latîfas. It then appears as the alter ego that “dwells in heaven” and acts directly upon its earthly self. At the sixth latîfa, the “Jesus of your being,” there is a distinct unveiling in which God manifests Himself through His attributes of Majesty and Beauty.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01873

The arcanum, or latîfa khafîya, is a luminous, transcendent, personal rûh, a special gift from God to those servants of whom He says: “In their hearts He has inscribed faith, and He supports them with a Spirit from Himself (bi-rûh min-ho)” (58:22). Semnâni understands this to mean: “He supports them with a Spirit that belongs to this faith. That is the hidden Spirit (rûh khafî),” meaning the Spirit of the latîfa khafîya. Elsewhere Semnâni adds: “In the words ‘with a Spirit from Himself’ lie sublime secrets that inspire sacred awe.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01874

“Let the believer fear for his faith, lest it be left without the help of a Spirit from Him—or the Spirit of that faith. If the faith inscribed in each soul”—the sacred inscription of faith from the beginning, the original religious disposition or fitra—“does not come to that soul's aid through a Spirit from Him, or through the Spirit of that faith, then its life beyond this life will be impossible.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01875

“So, believer, guard your faith carefully. Hold fast to the Friend of God”—the “Muhammad of your being,” the latîfa haqqîya—“so that the faith inscribed within you may be supported by a Spirit from Him.” This “Spirit from Him” is generally understood to mean the angel Gabriel. But there is more. In his Diarium, Semnâni bears witness to having seen this Spirit; and he immediately connects his experience with the Prophet's vision of the angel Gabriel and the distress the Prophet felt before gaining certainty.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01876

“Know with certainty,” he writes, “O seeker who aspires to certain knowledge, that for twenty-five years I have seen—I have been an eyewitness (ashâhido) to—my Rûh, my ‘Angel,’ in my visionary encounters (wâqi’ât), always in the same form. It never exchanges that form for another; it never changes. Sometimes, certainly, its form appears weaker, sometimes more intense; at times it seems to be suffering, at others to shine with strength. Its beauty increases as my actions become purer, and diminishes if some impurity casts a shadow over them.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01877

“Sometimes it reproaches me, and I too reproach it. When it is pleased with me, it receives me kindly, and I welcome it joyfully in return. If it were only a product of imagination, it would not persist so faithfully in one and the same form.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01878

During those twenty-five years, Semnâni had, of course, had time to become familiar with this spiritual companionship—for that is exactly what it was. These pages of the Diarium echo what we read in Najmoddîn Kobrâ and his disciples about the “witness in heaven,” the supersensible guide and companion (ostâd-e ghaybî).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01879

But at the beginning he had been seriously alarmed. That alarm is precisely why he appeals to the Prophet's experience: the Prophet, too, was profoundly shaken after seeing the Angel in his majestic form, “covering the whole horizon,” before becoming accustomed to his companionship in a form of human proportions.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01880

“When I first began to have this vision,” writes Semnâni, “the thought came to me that it was an imaginary fantasy brought on by strain upon the brain, the consequence of excessive spiritual practices and efforts. And who is safe from such a temptation? It came even to the prince of prophets himself, the beloved of God, at the beginning of his mission, so much so that he said to Khadija, his wife: ‘I am afraid I am going mad!’”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01881

Semnâni then recalls the famous episode. Khadija comforts the Prophet with the certainty of her own feminine intuition and takes him to her cousin Waraqa ibn Nûfal, the aged Christian Arab, the “great shaykh,” of whom tradition says that he had translated the Gospel into Arabic. Muhammad tells him of his vision, and Waraqa confirms that the being who came to him was indeed the “Supreme Nâmûs,” the one who had descended upon the earlier prophets, upon Moses and Jesus: that Nâmûs who is Gabriel, “the one who knows the secrets of the king.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01882

The word Nâmûs is a transcription of the Greek nomos, borrowed directly into Arabic. It occurs in an Arabic version of the Gospel of John, in verse 15:25, immediately before the reference to the coming of the Paraclete announced by Jesus. For Waraqa, Khadija's cousin and the “great shaykh,” Nâmûs is indeed the angel Gabriel. Islamic theology identifies Gabriel with the Holy Spirit, who descended upon Muhammad to invest him as the Paraclete foretold by Jesus, upon whom he had already descended.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01883

In Arabic the name Nâmûs acquires an additional resonance through its possible connection with the root n-m-s, “to keep a secret.” It means the confidant, “the one who knows the secrets of the king,” as Semnâni has just written, recalling Gabriel's traditional title, Rûh al-Amîn, the Faithful Spirit. The Ismaili encyclopedia of the “Brethren of Purity” (Ikhwân al-Safâ’) developed the notion of Nâmûs at considerable length. Nâmûs comes to mean the kingdom of the Spirit, the spiritual kingdom (mamlaka rûhânîya).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01884

Likewise, in its psychology, it denotes the highest of five categories of souls. Above the soul associated with philosophical wisdom, the soul of the intellect, stands the angelic or nâmûsian—that is, “Gabriel-like”—soul, the organ of prophetic wisdom. Here we are very close to what Semnâni calls the latîfa jabra’îlîya, the “Gabriel of your being,” who initiates the “Muhammad of your being.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01885

We can now understand why, when Semnâni describes seeing his Rûh, he is led to recall the Prophet's vision of the Angel: in both cases, the first alarm gives way to unshakable certainty. “Often, when I had first entered the spiritual path,” he says, “that same thought”—the thought that shook the Prophet—“came back to me, pressing upon me day after day, until my Lord favored me with inspiration and gave me the strength to drive it away by persevering in the dhikr, the remembrance of God. I waited until my soul found peace in contemplating Him and became like the first brightness of dawn.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01886

“Then there was no longer any room for doubt within me. If anyone wishes to be initiated into the events of the world of Mystery (’âlam al-ghayb), to contemplate them and perceive them intuitively, let him enter the way of the mystical travelers. Through sustained concentration of the heart (himma), they have crossed the deserts of existence, until ecstatic rapture has carried them into the tabernacles of glory. There they have tasted the drink of true spiritual knowledge, poured into the cup of love.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01887

We had asked whether Semnâni's Spiritual Diary could tell us more about what he calls the “angel Gabriel of your being,” the latîfa jabra’îlîya. We have seen him keep the secret at the decisive moment.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01888

Yet the indications brought together here confirm what we glimpsed earlier (§3). It does not seem possible to say more. We would, however, like to close these pages on the eminent visionary mystic ’Alâoddawleh Semnâni with a passage that sums up his Diarium. It appears at the end of his commentary on surah 54—the very surah that, a few pages back, opened our inquiry into the Diarium. This is one of the passages that best traces the course of his spiritual experience, expressed in the language of the latîfas and the “prophets of your being.” Every mystic inevitably experiences the rebellion of the people of each of these prophets: the natural faculties refusing to accept their prophet's message.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01889

“I myself experienced this state”—the rebellion of the “people of Noah”—“at the beginning of my spiritual life, when my father, my uncle, all my relatives, and my friends attributed to madness what they saw happening to me. For when I began practicing the effective and secret dhikr, then, on the very first night, there appeared to me blazing, radiant sparks, as though they were rising out of my chest to join the heavens.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01890

“When I lifted my eyelids and looked with my own eyes, I said to myself: ‘So everything they say about me is true!’ For a vision of sparks in the darkness of the night, inside a house plunged in darkness, surely could only come from a disorder of my brain. And my psychic faculties”—those belonging to the “Noah of my being”—“cried out that it was an imposture. They frightened me, trying to turn me away from the dhikr; the satanic powers inspired doubts in me about this vision of manifest Signs.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01891
“But my heart”—the “Abraham of my being”—“paid them no attention, and remained wholly absorbed in the dhikr until morning came.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01892

At dawn, then, the young man goes to the mosque. Yet when he takes his place on his prayer mat, brilliant stars appear before him and to his right, “in the direction of his qibla,” the direction of prayer. He is afraid, although inwardly he rejoices.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01893

But the satanic powers of his lower being trouble him, urging him to give up the dhikr. “I was so afraid of people's gossip,” he says, “that I did not dare breathe a word to anyone about what I had seen and contemplated with my own eyes.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01894

Until then, Semnâni had practiced the many traditional devotions customary in Sufism. Never before had he experienced these visions of light whose importance for his spiritual teaching we have now seen.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01895

But as soon as he received the secret of the dhikr from one of his brothers in religion (min akh lî fi’l-dîn), a disciple of the same shaykh, the visionary encounter occurred: the wâqi’a, the “Event,” which is the “approaching Hour” announced in the first verse of surah 54. At first he dares tell no one except his spiritual brother, Sharafoddîn Semnâni. Sharafoddîn then plays a role similar to that played for the Prophet by Khadija and the wise Waraqa. He rejoices and says with a smile:
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01896

“Glory to God, who has brought you to this secret vision, to the Signs that appear in the world of the Soul! I myself had to make pilgrimage for a whole year in the sanctuary of the Sacred Temple before these sparkling stars appeared to me on Mount ’Arafat. God has been generous to you in granting you the sight of these Signs after so short a time. Your duty now is to show gratitude to the divine Being: withdraw from ordinary company, and practice the dhikr according to the method you have now learned. For it will open the door of the heart to you, in sha’Allah—God willing.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01897

“Then I freed myself from the faculties that cried imposture and sought to raise doubts within me, and I devoted myself wholly to this dhikr. I chose solitude and retreat for two consecutive years, so that by the end of that time I had completed the full course of Moses' forty-day retreat. And behold, by His grace God opened to my heart what no eye has seen, what no ear has heard, and what has never entered the heart of any human being.”
